descriptor: Hot-mix asphalt, aggregates & highway construction roll-up · reported in USD

charts.title: Gross Profit, Operating Income & Net Income
Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Construction Partners, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: ROAD is a roll-up -- most of its growth since FY2023 has come from acquiring paving and aggregates businesses, not from winning more work in existing markets. See the "Revenue Growth: Organic vs. Acquired" chart below for the split.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality (paving season runs spring-fall)

growthMix.title: Organic vs. acquired revenue growth
growthMix.content:
Construction Partners discloses revenue growth as two components: existing-markets (organic) revenue increase -- more volume and pricing in markets it already served -- and acquisition revenue -- sales added by businesses it bought during or since the prior period. The organic growth % line is organic increase divided by prior-period revenue in the same markets.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: FY2025's $835m of acquisition revenue dwarfs the $153m of organic increase -- the roll-up strategy (it closed over a dozen bolt-on deals that year) is doing almost all the work. Organic growth itself has stayed in a steady 7-9% band, so the multiple the market pays is really a bet on management's ability to keep sourcing and integrating deals at a reasonable price, not on faster same-market growth.

What to watch:

  • Acquisition revenue falling faster than the deal pipeline would suggest (integration or availability problems)
  • Organic growth % decelerating below the historical band -- would mean the base business is slowing even as acquisitions keep headline revenue up
  • Goodwill and intangibles on the balance sheet growing with each deal (see Balance Sheet chart)

plantNetwork.title: Plant & facility network
plantNetwork.content:
Construction Partners discloses the count of hot-mix asphalt (HMA) plants, aggregates (crushed stone/sand/gravel) facilities and liquid asphalt terminals it operates at each fiscal year-end -- the physical footprint that both makes and consumes its own raw materials.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: HMA plant count jumped 67 → 84 → 109 and aggregates facilities 13 → 17 → 17 over FY2023-FY2025, almost entirely through acquisition (see the growth-mix chart) rather than new builds. Vertical integration -- owning the aggregates that feed its own asphalt plants -- is the vertical-integration margin story management cites every quarter.

What to watch:

  • Plant/facility counts growing without a matching lift in gross margin (integration not yet realised)
  • FY-only data -- the count is disclosed at fiscal year-end, not quarterly

backlog.title: Backlog composition
backlog.content:
Total backlog is the dollar value of work awarded but not yet completed. Construction Partners splits it into uncompleted (awarded) backlog -- contracts formally signed -- and low-bid backlog -- work where ROAD was the low bidder but the contract is not yet executed, a leading but less certain indicator.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: backlog roughly doubled from $1.6bn (FY2023) to $3.4bn (Q3 2026), giving several quarters of revenue visibility ahead -- state DOT paving work is typically multi-year. A rising low-bid share signals future awards still to convert; a rising uncompleted share signals work already locked in but not yet executed.

What to watch:

  • Backlog growth outpacing revenue growth (visibility improving) or vice versa
  • Low-bid backlog that never converts to uncompleted (lost or delayed awards)
  • Backlog concentration in state DOT funding cycles

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Construction Partners, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
